limitations: B402 Bazaar's documentation describes l30DaysTotalCalls, l30DaysUniquePayers and fail_rate_24h on a resource. The public discovery responses do not carry them: across /bazaar/resources, /bazaar/search and /bazaar/merchant the union of returned keys is resource, type, x402Version, description, accepts and lastUpdated. Payer counts are therefore shown as not served rather than as zero.

A Bazaar listing states what a merchant declared, not what the endpoint answers. Where our own call gets a different network or asset than the listing advertises, the row shows the challenge we actually received and flags the disagreement.

Resources with a 24-hour failure rate above 50% are filtered out by the Bazaar before we see them, so this catalogue is already survivorship-biased in the merchant's favour. Our own probe is the correction.

Reading registrations from the chain stops about 0.6 days back, where the free BSC providers stop serving eth_getLogs. This crawl therefore accumulates new registrations each cycle rather than walking history; older ones are unread rather than absent. Setting ARCHIVE_RPC_URL removes the limit.

examples.what: Somebody added liquidity to PancakeSwap V3 position 6801109.
examples.teaches: This is what the second half of a recentre looks like: liquidity going back in around the current price. An agent hired for this job does it when the fees it would collect are worth more than the gas and the loss of moving.

examples.what: Somebody supplied capital to a Venus market — the move a yield agent makes when a better net rate is worth the gas.
examples.teaches: Supplying is the easy half. The job is deciding whether the extra rate pays back this transaction's gas before the rate changes again — which is why the board measures switching payback in days rather than counting moves.

examples.what: A borrower repaid part of their own Venus loan — exactly the action a health-factor agent takes, before the threshold rather than after.
examples.teaches: Doing this early costs gas. Not doing it costs the ten percent liquidation penalty Venus charges. The whole job is the gap between those two numbers.

examples.what: A swap filled on the PancakeSwap V3 WBNB/USDT pool — one leg of the kind of ladder a grid maintains.
examples.teaches: A grid is a ladder of these. Note that the event comes from the pool and not from the router — the routers emit nothing at all, which is why a capability scan that watches a router finds nothing however much an agent trades.

counterfactual.positionNote: A synthetic position: 1000 of USDT and the matching amount of the other side, opened in a ±60-tick band around the price at block 120538348. It is nobody's real position — connecting a wallet and replaying against one somebody actually holds is the next step.

rows.name: Hold
rows.describes: Does nothing at all. The honest do-nothing arm every other row has to beat.

rows.name: Range Keeper I
rows.describes: Keeps a wide band around the price and only moves when the price has stayed outside it. Trades fee density for fewer, cheaper interventions.

rows.name: Range Keeper II
rows.describes: A tighter band than Range Keeper I, moved when the price has been outside it for a while. More fee density, more recentres.

rows.name: Tight Band Keeper
rows.describes: Holds a narrow band and recentres almost as soon as the price leaves it. Maximises time in range and pays gas for every move — often more than the extra fees are worth.
